articles.title: An iron mine worked in North Carolina from the 1820s to the 1930s now shelters five bat species; a conservancy has bought 320 surrounding acres to protect the tunnels and the recovering forest above them
articles.summary: A former iron mine in North Carolina, which operated for more than 100 years, has become an important shelter for five species of bats.
articles.body: A former iron mine in North Carolina, which operated for more than 100 years, has become an important shelter for five species of bats. Its underground tunnels now provide places for bats to hibernate, including species that are rare and endangered. To protect this habitat and the forest surrounding it, a conservation group has purchased 320 acres of land around the historic mine.The Southern Appalachian Highlands Conservancy (SAHC) bought the property in 2026. It includes the site of the historic Cranberry Iron Mine, located just south of Elk Park in Avery County. The land also contains parts of Cranberry Creek, a wild trout stream, along with smaller water sources. The protected area reaches elevations of around 3,900 feet along its western ridgeline.According to SAHC, the mine was used to extract iron ore from around 1826 until the 1930s. Initially, most of the mining took place on the surface. However, underground mining began in the 1880s, following the arrival of the Eastern Tennessee and Western North Carolina railroad from Johnson City in 1882. The railway helped mining operations expand in the area.Although mining eventually stopped, the underground passages continued to serve a different purpose. They became important shelters for five bat species: Virginia big-eared bats, tri-coloured bats, little brown bats, big brown bats and northern long-eared bats. The latest land purchase will strengthen protection of these underground habitats and the forest above them.How the former mine became a bat habitatThe North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission (NCWRC) had taken steps to protect the mine's bat population before the latest purchase. In 2002, it bought the mineral rights to the Cranberry Iron Mine and received a donated conservation easement. This arrangement was intended to protect the hibernating bats living inside the underground passages.However, the earlier conservation agreement did not cover every activity on the property. It protected the underground bat habitat but still allowed commercial timber harvesting and the construction of media towers. The land was substantially logged between 2008 and 2010, when a hardwood manufacturing company owned the property.SAHC's purchase has now brought additional land around the protected mine habitat under conservation. The organisation plans to manage the recovering forest to improve its long-term health and maintain wildlife habitat.“This property tells a story of Appalachia from the 1800s when iron ore was mined and transported on the historic Tweetsie Railroad,” says Land Protection Director Michelle Pugliese. “The evolution of the former mine to become a safe haven for endangered bats demonstrates nature’s ability to recover and adapt. I am excited to partner with the NC Wildlife Resources Commission to safeguard that habitat.”Why protecting bat habitats mattersBats play an important role in maintaining ecosystems and also provide benefits to humans. They help pollinate plants and control populations of pest insects. They can also help prevent the spread of mosquito-borne diseases. A nursing female bat can catch up to 4,500 mosquitoes in a single night.Bats generally become visible while searching for food during the early evening and early morning, although they remain active throughout the night. They use echolocation to navigate and locate their prey, but they also have good eyesight.According to Katherine Etchison, statewide bat biologist for NCWRC, bats in North Carolina mate during spring or autumn and usually give birth to one young bat each year. Some species form maternity colonies during summer to raise their young, while others live and raise their offspring alone.Several species migrate south during winter. Others remain in sheltered places called hibernacula, where they sleep through the colder months. Caves and abandoned mines are among their preferred hibernation sites. Bats can also use buildings and bridges for shelter and generally return to the same location every year when possible.Some bat species can live for 20 to 30 years in the wild. North Carolina is home to 17 bat species, of which three are federally endangered and one is federally threatened.White-nose syndrome poses a serious threatDespite their ecological importance, native bat populations are declining. They face threats from pesticides, habitat loss and disturbances at maternity colonies and hibernation sites. One of the most serious dangers is white-nose syndrome (WNS), a fungal disease that affects bats during hibernation.The disease gets its name from the white fungal growth that appears on infected bats' muzzles. The fungus damages their wings, which are important not only for flying but also for functions such as heat exchange, circulation and maintaining water balance.The fungus grows in cold conditions and causes bats to use up their stored fat during hibernation. As their energy reserves run out, they can die from starvation. Since WNS was first detected in the US in 2006, it has killed millions of bats. Its spread has been confirmed in 42 states and nine Canadian provinces. The disease was detected in North Carolina in 2011.Kyle Shute, SAHC's land protection associate, said protecting undisturbed winter shelters was important for bat survival. Keeping people away from these areas also helps reduce disturbance and the risk of spreading the fungal spores.The fungus can spread through direct contact with infected bats and through contaminated environments where they roost or hibernate. People can accidentally carry it on their shoes, clothes and equipment.Mine entrances closed to prevent disturbanceTo protect the bats, NCWRC and the US Forest Service have installed steel gates at the mine entrances. These gates allow bats to move freely in and out while preventing people from entering the tunnels.SAHC and NCWRC staff also take precautions when monitoring the habitat to avoid spreading white-nose syndrome. The organisations have fenced off the mine site and put up signs stating that the area is permanently closed to the public. They are also working to address trespassing on the protected property.“NCWRC has erected clear fencing and signage to let people know that the area is permanently closed to the public,” says Roan Stewardship Director Marquette Crockett. “We will cooperate and partner with NCWRC to ensure the area remains strictly closed, due to the sensitive nature of habitat and bat species.”Researchers have also used the Cranberry Iron Mine to study ways to improve bat survival despite white-nose syndrome. One initiative, called the Fat Bat project, tested whether attracting insects to concentrated areas could provide bats with more food before winter hibernation and after they emerge in spring.The idea was to create a concentrated feeding area, described as a 'bug buffet', so bats could build up their fat reserves. Research has shown that bats with more stored fat are significantly more likely to survive winter.NCWRC continues to monitor bats across North Carolina to track the spread of white-nose syndrome, identify their distribution and hibernation sites, and estimate population trends. Its biologists have surveyed thousands of bats with the help of partner organisations to guide habitat and land management efforts.SAHC says it will continue working with NCWRC and researchers to protect the mine habitat and support efforts to recover regional bat populations.You use AI every day. articles.title: Senegal human rights group demands government action after deadly sinking
articles.summary: Thousands ⁠of people have ⁠died in recent years attempting to reach Spain’s Canary Islands from West Africa.
articles.body:
A human rights group in Senegal is calling on the government to launch a parliamentary inquiry after a small boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of the West African country, killing at least 39 people.

In a statement, Action for Human Rights and Friendship (ADHA) denounced a “lack of lasting results” to reduce migrant deaths at sea.

“Despite 300 thousand euros [$336,000] announced for the Navy and the training of more than 300 agents, the association denounces the lack of lasting results in the face of the increase in irregular arrivals to the Canaries,” ADHA said.

The pirogue-type flat-bottomed boat departed from Saint-Louis in northern Senegal and was headed to the Spanish coast when it overturned off the Lompoul dunes, in the Kebemer department, 180km (112 miles) north of the capital Dakar, on Sunday, state media said.

ADHA said, “It is no longer enough to deplore shipwrecks, announce measures and count interceptions.”

Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye offered condolences and pledged to clamp down on traffickers behind the dangerous journeys.

Initial reports put the death toll at 21, but more bodies were found as emergency services continued search and rescue efforts, raising the number of dead first to 34, then to 39.

Only one passenger was rescued alive, and several others are still believed to be missing.

“The boat was carrying people seeking to migrate irregularly”, Senegal’s Ministry of the Interior and Public Security said in a statement, but did not specify how many people were on board the vessel at the time.

Thousands ⁠of people have ⁠died in recent years attempting to reach Spain’s Canary Islands from West Africa, including ‌635 in the first five months of this year, according to ‌migrant rights ‌group Walking Borders.

Spanish authorities on the Canary Island of El Hierro declared an emergency on Saturday after a surge in migrant boat arrivals.

El Hierro authorities said more than 3,300 people had arrived on board about 30 boats since the start of November.

articles.title: Trump says Iran is sealed off. But can new US task force stop weapons flow?
articles.summary: Analysts say a small intelligence-focused unit cannot seal Iran’s borders, and others warn it could expand the war.
articles.body:
It was another bold statement from United States President Donald Trump: An edict in his usual inflated style, claiming that the US had almost sealed Iran off from the rest of the world.

“Very little gets into, or out of, Iran!” the US president posted on his Truth Social account on Sunday, a day after the US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced its latest plan to choke Tehran’s military supply networks.

On Sunday, CENTCOM announced Task Force Iron Gate – a unit targeting land routes and the Caspian Sea, which will aim to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials.

Trump’s message on Truth Social claimed that the task force was “in full force and effect” in Iran – and that between this and the US naval blockade of the strategic Strait of Hormuz, the US had virtually cut off what enters and exits the country.

But analysts say a small intelligence-focused unit cannot seal Iran’s borders or stop its extensive procurement networks without regional cooperation.

They did warn, however, that attempts to disrupt these networks could draw neighbouring countries into the conflict and undermine ongoing diplomatic efforts in the US-Israel war on Iran.

“I see Task Force Iron Gate as a desperate attempt to extend the American naval blockade into Iran’s continental supply networks without deploying American troops along its borders,” Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of defence studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.

Task Force Iron Gate aims to find out where “weapons systems are coming in, how they could potentially be cut off” and how “Iran is transporting its energy”, Michael Mulroy, a former US deputy assistant defence secretary for the Middle East, has told Al Jazeera.

Based in Tampa, Florida, the unit will coordinate with other US government agencies “on preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea”, CENTCOM has said.

Analysts said the task force could coordinate sanctions enforcement, pressure foreign suppliers, and work with partner countries to disrupt smuggling.

According to Matthew Savill, director of military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute, the US mission would rely on a combination of satellite imagery, drones, intercepted communications, financial intelligence and intelligence-sharing.

“Then, frankly, I would expect some use of force – strikes or discreet ground operations – to confiscate components, whether done by US forces or the Israelis,” the analyst told Al Jazeera.

“They would want to pass some intelligence on and bring legal and economic pressure to bear outside the Middle East if they think dual-use components are coming from the West … but if the target is supplies from Russia and China, that will be tougher.”

While CENTCOM’s announcement did not explicitly identify Iran’s weapons trade with Russia, analysts say the unit could be seen as an attempt to disrupt supply networks that include Russian connections.

US media have reported that Russia has sent drone components and explosives to Iran via the Caspian Sea . There are also claims that Russian technology could be helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles.

Krieg agreed the task force would combine methods, but stated that it would operate largely as an “intelligence fusion cell”.

“Twenty people cannot police thousands of kilometres of frontiers,” he said.

“The objective is not necessarily to stop every shipment, but to make Iranian military procurement progressively more expensive, slower and riskier,” he added.

The obstacle the US mission will face, however, is political rather than technological, he argued. Iran’s neighbours will be largely unwilling to cooperate.

“Iraq offers Washington some leverage, but Iranian-aligned networks remain deeply embedded in its economy and security institutions,” he explained.

Azerbaijan could cooperate discreetly, while Turkmenistan would be “extremely reluctant” to jeopardise its neutrality or relationships with Russia and China, said the professor.

Pakistan is particularly unlikely to participate openly because it is currently mediating between Washington and Tehran, he added. Turkiye also has little interest in turning its border with Iran into another confrontation, said Krieg.

“Without these countries’ cooperation, Washington can disrupt individual networks but cannot effectively seal Iran’s borders,” he said.

Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut and a non-resident senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, has previously told Al Jazeera that Iran’s history as a trading nation for thousands of years makes the US mission near impossible.

“There’s an enormous web of contacts that Iran has had for thousands of years with traders and partners and allies all over the region, especially in Asia – it’s virtually impossible for the US to seal off every one,” he said.

“There are people all over the region who have links with Iran, some very close, some just commercial,” he said.

Krieg expressed concern about the potential for mission creep — that the task force’s action could widen the war to new arenas.

“Intelligence gathering can quickly become pressure for seizures, border closures or military strikes against suspected logistical infrastructure,” he said.

“This would extend America’s economic war into the sovereign territory of neighbouring states.”

Iran’s response in turn would likely be asymmetrical, “intensifying maritime coercion in Hormuz and potentially using the Houthis to increase pressure around Bab al-Mandeb and Saudi Arabia”, Krieg added.

Joe Kent, a former top US counterterrorism official, has also argued that the new task force is an attempt by CENTCOM to subvert ongoing diplomatic efforts.

“This is CENTCOM inviting Iran to escalate while the vice president is attempting to negotiate with the Iranians,” Kent, who resigned in March in protest against the US’s war on Iran, said on X following the US military’s announcement.

“This is, as CENTCOM calls it, ‘policy by CONOP’, when the military finds a way to subvert the White House without blatantly disobeying the President, by taking actions that will ensure a war escalates or perpetuates.”

The Wall Street Journal, meanwhile, has reported that CENTCOM chief Brad Cooper is among the many officials, alongside Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, pressing Trump to renew attacks on Iran.

Some analysts, however, argue that without US access to the Caspian Sea, troops on the ground, or cooperation from neighbouring states, the task force will have limited practical impact.

Mahjoob Zweiri, a professor of contemporary history and politics at Qatar University, has told Al Jazeera that the new initiative may just be symbolic because of the lack of US military presence on the Caspian Sea.

“America has no access to the sea, unless some of the neighbouring countries like Azerbaijan or Armenia or others collaborate [with them] … And they’re not collaborating on this because they don’t want to upset Russia,” said Zweiri. “It will require … troops on the ground, and this is unlikely to happen.”

articles.title: Between the chip and the slip: Honeytrap suspicions further sours ties between US and China
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: China has been chipping away at American technological primacy for years.
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: China has been chipping away at American technological primacy for years. Now, if US intelligence suspicions are borne out, it may have found a rather intimate way of getting close to the crown jewels of America's AI empire – seducing its top chip honcho, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, in a honeytrap operation worthy of a spy thriller.The allegations are explosive, although they remain unproven. Nvidia's board, which includes Aarti Shah, an Indian-origin veteran from Eli Lilly, has launched an independent investigation into whether its 63-year-old chief executive was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Beijing has denied the allegations, saying they are "nothing but smears against China."The flap comes at a particularly awkward time for the two countries, with President Trump scheduled to meet the Chinese president Xi Jinping next week (on November 18-19) on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering in Shenzhen, a city that is emblematic of China's own technological ambitions.Asked about Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese spy, Trump told reporters on Air Force One that the Nvidia chief is an “honorable guy" who has done an "amazing job for our country" and he probably has as “excuse" that needs to be heard."I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what is going on," Trump said, while appearing to give him the benefit of doubt by asserting Huang should remain Nvidia CEO and he would probably take him on his Asia trip.Huang, meanwhile, has admitted to an affair with a business executive identified as Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials reportedly believe was collecting information for China. In a message to Nvidia employees, he wrote: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a former television journalist in China who subsequently is said to have reinvented herself as a semiconductor industry power broker. She became a senior executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, a data-centre company that emerged as one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia.According to industry reports, Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over two years. Its position in the regional semiconductor supply chain is particularly sensitive because Southeast Asia is seen as an important transit point in the suspected diversion of advanced American chips to China, where their sale is restricted by Washington.US intelligence officials reportedly concluded that Alice Huang had been recruited by Chinese intelligence to cultivate a relationship with Jensen Huang, obtain information, and potentially influence access to Nvidia's advanced processors. The precise nature of the information allegedly sought, and whether anything of strategic value was actually obtained, remain unclear.Jensen Huang himself has consistently argued that completely shutting China out of the US semiconductor ecosystem is strategically counterproductive. He has lobbied Trump to permit sales of less advanced Nvidia products to Chinese customers, arguing that American companies should not surrender the world's largest technology market to domestic Chinese competitors. The lobbying has had some success, with Trump allowing Nvidia to sell H200 processors to China under a revised export framework.All this places Huang in an unusual position: he is simultaneously America's most important AI industry champion and one of the most influential corporate advocates for retaining access to China. The espionage allegations now threaten to complicate that balancing act considerably.The Nvidia board meanwhile has appointed a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside legal counsel, to examine the matter. Its initial statement was carefully calibrated: it had "no reason to believe" that either American national security or Nvidia's secrets had been compromised, but would examine all available information. It also expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team.On his part, Huang has pledged full cooperation with the board's investigation, declaring his commitment to protecting Nvidia and supporting American national security. He also described himself as proud and grateful to be an American.Huang is not just another corporate CEO; he is Nvidia's chief strategist, chief salesman, and public face of the AI revolution. His leather jacket has become almost as recognisable in technology circles as the company's green logo and his ability to navigate Washington – where he has had conspicuous access to President Trump – Silicon Valley and Asian technology markets has been central to Nvidia's extraordinary rise.He has also met PM Modi several times, most recently at the Nvidia's multi-day AI summit in Mumbai last month. In fact, by Huang's own account, his first meeting with PM Modi was in 2018 when the Indian PM surprised him by inviting him to speak directly to the Indian Cabinet about the future and importance of artificial intelligence long before AI became a mainstream global discussion.Meanwhile, US lawmakers in Washington, chuffed by mid-term elections results that have significantly dimmed executive primacy, are already demanding answers. House Foreign Affairs Committee chairman Brian Mast, China Select Committee chairman John Moolenaar and Intelligence Committee chairman Rick Crawford have asked Huang to brief them behind closed doors on November 18 about the allegations and Nvidia's safeguards against foreign espionage. The coincidence of that proposed briefing with the approaching Trump-Xi encounter adds another layer of awkwardness to the meeting between the two leaders that was already visible when Xi came on a state visit to Washington DC late September.You use AI every day. articles.title: Action on energy costs is my overriding aim, says Fahnbulleh
articles.summary: The energy secretary says reducing bills is key to maintaining public support for climate action.
articles.body:
The energy secretary has stressed that affordability is her "overriding objective", as she said reducing bills would be key to maintaining public support for climate action.

Speaking to BBC Panorama, Miatta Fahnbulleh insisted that the government's drive for cleaner power would help to cut energy bills in the long term.

But she conceded that the push to reduce carbon emissions was currently "under pressure" amid discontent at rising prices in recent years.

It comes as ministers grapple with how to respond to a predicted surge in energy prices in January, expected to mark the biggest rise in bills for four years.

Scientists predict 2026 hottest year on record as climate talks begin

Government's EV targets expected to be reduced this week

Labour has faced extra political pressure over its climate ambitions since coming to power, as Reform UK rose in opinion polls and the Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch disowned their previous ambition of reaching net zero by 2050.

Both opposition parties have taken particular aim at public subsidy schemes designed to boost renewable sources of electricity generation, arguing that the drive for cleaner energy has driven up costs for consumers.

UK households currently pay one of the highest rates for electricity in Europe.

Bills have increased due to subsidies but also because of the high price of gas (a fossil fuel) driven up by international conflicts.

Asked during her Panorama interview what her main task was, Fahnbulleh replied: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."

In the interview, which was recorded last week, and aired on Monday night, she argued that Labour's push for greener electricity was "one of our routes to delivering affordability".

"The drive to clean power is about decoupling our dependence on global fossil fuel markets," she added. "Ultimately if we have homegrown renewables, nuclear, that's the way in which we will drive bills in the long term."

However, she conceded that struggles over energy affordability were part of the reason the consensus on climate action was "under pressure".

"People want to blame net zero for that. Now, I don't believe that's the case.

"But I'm very clear that part of the way in which we build and maintain public consent is that we've got to show that this transition, which we have to do on climate grounds, is good for people's pockets."

The UK had a record number of heatwaves this summer and suffered successive damaging wildfires, which the Met Office has said was made 130 times more likely by climate change .

Just last month, whilst hosting the UK's first summit on wildfires, Andy Burnham acknowledged that as a result of climate change "the summer we've just had is likely to be a more regular situation going forward".

But he has also vowed to lead a "cost of living government" and reindustralise the economy.

This has prompted some in Westminster to speculate that he could demote climate action to help reduce energy costs in the short-term.

His government has dismayed some green activists by diverting funding from the energy department to help meet defence funding targets, including money previously earmarked for energy efficiency schemes.

Last month the government approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field which also prompted criticism from some campaigners, although ministers have sought to argue it will minimise imports of higher emission fuels.

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, located off the coast of Shetland.

Speaking to Panorama, Fahnbulleh insisted reducing carbon emissions "absolutely is a priority", pointing to this summer's droughts as evidence of the need to tackle global warming.

However, she conceded that Labour's target for 95% of electricity generated in Britain to come from clean power sources by 2030 was a "stretch".

On Monday, it was reported that the government is considering weakening the electric vehicle mandate requiring car manufacturers to phase out production of petrol and diesel cars by 2035.

This could prove a blow to not only the country's climate targets but the UK's claim to be providing leadership on the issues just as ministers head to Turkey for COP31, the UN's climate summit.

articles.title: Israel’s Shin Bet finds no evidence of foreign election meddling: Report
articles.summary: Netanyahu and Zini’s interference claims lack evidence, according to law enforcement officials quoted by Haaretz.
articles.body:
Israel’s Shin Bet has failed to find evidence of foreign interference in last month’s elections, despite claims from the domestic security agency’s chief, David Zini, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the newspaper Haaretz has reported.

Two senior Israeli law enforcement officials said that the investigation, which is still ongoing, has found no evidence that several hundred thousand shekels had been transferred from the Palestinian Authority (PA) to Arab-led parties in Israel, Haaretz reported on Monday.

There were no transfers from Qatar or any other Arab country being investigated. That’s despite allegations from Netanyahu’s party, Likud, that money had been transferred to boost turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, without the party providing any tangible evidence to support its claims.

The allegations continue a long-running anti-Qatar campaign in Israel that predates the election. Haaretz has previously reported that a secret campaign involving Israeli influence expets and political advisers targeted Qatar in the weeks after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks.

Qatar has denied all the allegations of interference, and called them unsubstantiated.

The latest claims from Zini and Netanyahu intensified in the wake of the strong electoral performance by the parties, led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, in the October 27 elections. Their 19 seats, confirmed by Israel’s election authorities , mean that Jewish parties opposed to Netanyahu have enough seats in parliament to force the prime minister out, if they are willing to work with the Arab-led parties.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog has tasked opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot with making the first attempt to form a government, possibly spelling the end of Netanyahu’s time as prime minister.

“[It is] certainly not a security matter, and it is highly doubtful that it is even a criminal one,” one of the officials quoted by Haaretz said.

“All there is is intelligence information without any real substantiation,” another quote attributed to one of the officials said.

Dozens of people have been questioned, but no evidence has so far been found of money being transferred. Haaretz also found that major fuel companies in Israel found no unusual activity involving fuel cards, undermining the allegation that Arab voters had been bribed with fuel cards in exchange for their votes.

Zini, who was selected by Netanyahu to lead Shin Bet last year and is regarded as an ally of the Israeli leader, has sought to investigate several leading politicians who are Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Netanyahu also questioned why Ahmad Tibi, a leading Arab politician in Israel, visited Qatar a few days ahead of the election.

Tibi explained that his trip to Doha was to appear on Al Jazeera.

Qatar has denied the unsubstantiated allegations of interference or funding of any activities aimed at influencing the Israeli election results.

“We reject the accusations made by certain Israeli politicians and their contacts in the media, who have launched yet another disinformation campaign aiming to drag Qatar into Israeli political disputes following this week’s elections,” Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Majed al-Ansari said in a social media post on October 29.

Israel’s attorney general Gali Baharav-Miara said on Sunday that she had seen no evidence from the investigation of anything that would have influenced the election results “or substantiate a claim of influence that could lead to a change in the election results”.

Israeli police and Shin Bet are expected to submit their assessments to Baharav-Miara in the next few days, the report said.

articles.title: France blames Iran for ‘unprecedented’ supermarket fridge cyberattack
articles.summary: France is blaming Iran for last month’s supermarket refrigerator cyberattack. which spoiled produce at around 700 retailers, and is vowing to slap sanctions on Tehran in response.
articles.body: France is blaming Iran for last month’s supermarket refrigerator cyberattack. which spoiled produce at around 700 retailers, and is vowing to slap sanctions on Tehran in response. “This was an attack of unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggressiveness,” Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told reporters Monday. He described it as the first large-scale cyberattack carried out for sabotage purposes on French national territory. “It represents a major assault on the nation’s interests and on the security of the French people,” Barrot said. France has summoned Iran’s ambassador and intends to impose retaliatory sanctions “at a European level,” he added. There was no immediate comment from Tehran on the French allegations. The cyberattack in October occurred when hackers remotely connected to supermarket refrigerators and freezers, then raised their temperature by switching on defrost cycles, according to CNN affiliate BFMTV. That led to the loss of large quantities of fresh and frozen produce and even caused some of the refrigeration equipment to catch fire. The Paris prosecutor’s office took up the case and on Monday accused Iran of being behind the attack, citing “the use of Farsi and IP addresses pointing to devices located in Iran.” The prosecutor’s office said it has opened an investigation into the head of Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, as well as his two deputies and any other individuals responsible. A similar cyberattack targeted supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium and Ireland earlier this month, though it remains unclear if the incidents are linked to the one in France. No one has claimed responsibility for this month’s cyberattacks in other European countries. Shortly after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in late February, the US intelligence community issued a flurry of private warnings to American companies and government agencies urging vigilance amid the threat of possible cyberattacks from Iran, according to national security sources and memos reviewed by CNN. This story has been updated.

articles.title: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
articles.summary: Tons of chilled and frozen food was spoiled last month as fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets heated up.
articles.body:
France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers across the country last month.

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions.

Iran has yet to respond officially, but some Iranian media outlets have dismissed the allegations as baseless.

The French hacking, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen anc chilled food in France was followed by a similar attack against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.

Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".

He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".

France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.

The Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.

Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.

Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.

In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.

If the IRGC carried out the cyber-attacks, it remains unclear whether they were part of Iran's deterrence strategy.

On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.

More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.

Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.

The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.

Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.

Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.

Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.

In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.

The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.

articles.title: 19 runners in California marathon hospitalized with ‘unusual symptoms,’ prompting police probe
articles.summary: Multiple half-marathon participants in Santa Barbara went to the hospital with “unusual symptoms” after the event on Sunday, prompting a police investigation.
articles.body: Multiple half-marathon participants in Santa Barbara went to the hospital with “unusual symptoms” after the event on Sunday, prompting a police investigation. The participants seeking medical treatment arrived at Santa Barbara and Goleta Valley Cottage Hospitals by ambulance, self-transportation or as walk-ins, according to the Santa Barbara Police Department. It’s unclear what the symptoms were or what caused them. In a statement to NBC News, Cottage Health said a “larger than expected” number of emergency visits were linked to Sunday’s run. “This morning 19 participants arrived at Cottage EDs, a number of them with similar symptoms of undetermined cause,” Cottage Health said, in part. “We are working to determine whether this is due to the heat or other factors.” David Monico, the event director for the Santa Barbara Half Marathon, said in an interview with NBC Los Angeles that Sunday’s race had more transports than in past years, possibly due to the warm weather and an increase in participants. “In years past, we’ve had overcast skies or less warm temperatures this time of year, so we have not had this many transports, but there’s always a handful,” he said. “But this year, it was more than we’ve had in the past. We also had more runners than we’ve had in the past as well.” Monico said the event’s medical team, who were set up throughout the course, reported seeing typical symptoms for endurance events, such as heat exhaustion, regular exhaustion and dehydration. “There was a lot that has been said on social media and was circulated, and so (the police are) doing their due diligence to see if there’s any facts and truth behind it,” he said. “We don’t know at this point. All we know is that from our medical team and what has been reported so far is that there weren’t any unusual symptoms or circumstances for those that have been transported that you typically see at events like this.” Police say the general public does not need to take any specific action at this time but that people who feel ill should seek medical help. Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact Santa Barbara police Sgt. Andre Miller at 805-897-2330. The annual event started at 7 a.m. and had 7,500 registered participants, according to race organizers. “Our wish is that everybody gets safe from point A to point B,” Monico said. “For friends and family of those that had been transported and were hospitalized, we feel for them. We want them to come home safely.”

articles.title: Del Boy or Custard Cream? People asked to suggest capybara names
articles.summary: Curraghs Wildlife Park seeks names based on biscuits, Only Fools and Horses, Manx places or South America.
articles.body:
People are being asked to suggest names for eight capybara pups that were born on the Isle of Man five weeks ago.

The manager at Curraghs Wildlife Park said naming animals helped people "identify" with them and "care about what is happening to them in the wild".

Kathleen Graham said the five boys and three girls would be named around four themes, either Manx place names, South American names, biscuit names or Only Fools and Horses characters.

Graham said the latter was just for "fun", "we all love biscuits", and "with it being the year of the Manx language, we thought Manx place names would be good or even the south American names as capybaras are from there".

Graham said it was very important for bonds to form, especially when you are talking about species conservation.

"Capybaras in themselves are not endangered, however animals that share the habitat with them are and so through donations, raised for the capybara, we have been able to donate from our conservation funds towards projects like tapirs," she said.

"People connect when they know an individual animal and they are then more likely to care about what is happening to them in the wild."

The arrival of the pups has prompted the Isle of Man attraction to extend its opening hours.

The park would usually reduce its opening hours during the colder months to four days a week, but has retained its longer summer schedule to give people more chance to see the new arrivals.

Graham said the pups had "proven to be quite popular" with visitors and visitor numbers for 2026 are expected to increase to more than 50,000.

Once the animals are bigger the park will look to re-introduce the capybara experience where people can interact with them, she said.

Since the announcement of the eight pups on the island, other places in the UK like Edinburgh Zoo and Hertfordshire Zoo have announced their own arrival of pups.

Graham said while these rodents were "not managed at a high level" like red pandas or humble penguins, the zoos coordinated to ensure there was a good population.

"Together we coordinated a few moves and that is why people will notice quite a few zoos in the UK have announced capybara pups around the same time, but the Isle of Man has the biggest number with eight."

articles.title: An Oregon couple in their 70s were wrongly said to have moved out of their own home, which was sold at foreclosure in 2022 though they never left; a jury has now awarded them over $8 million against the firms involved
articles.summary: An Oregon couple in their 70s have been awarded more than $8 million after a jury found that companies involved in the foreclosure of their home had
articles.body: An Oregon couple in their 70s have been awarded more than $8 million after a jury found that companies involved in the foreclosure of their home had committed unlawful trade practices and financial abuse. The couple, Wallace Owen and Barbara Owen, had continued living in the property even after the loan companies claimed they had moved out.According to Exlitem, a legal research platform, the house, located on Skyline Road South in Salem, Oregon, was sold at a foreclosure auction in September 2022. The sale went ahead even though the couple had not left the property. The buyer, Lantern Gate Properties, later filed a lawsuit seeking to remove them from the house.The dispute began after American Advisors Group (AAG), which serviced the couple's reverse mortgage, claimed in 2021 that they had moved out. AAG was acting on behalf of Reverse Mortgage Funding, the company that held the mortgage deed. The loan companies treated the claim as a default and began foreclosure proceedings.However, the couple had continued to use the property as their home. The report said the companies did not inspect it to establish whether they had actually moved. The foreclosure process also went ahead despite postal tracking records showing that legal notices sent to Wallace Owen had not reached the homeowners.A jury in Marion County, Oregon, delivered its verdict in January this year. It found Clear Recon Corp and Aldridge Pite LLP liable on several claims involving the foreclosure and the handling of money left over from the property sale. AAG had earlier been found liable by default for financial abuse of a vulnerable person. The jury determined the damages payable by the companies.How the foreclosure beganWallace and Barbara Owen bought the Salem property in 2015, and used it as their primary residence. Barbara transferred her legal interest in the property to Wallace in 2017. Both were over 65 that year and continued living in the house.Wallace had taken a reverse mortgage using the property as security for the loan. Reverse Mortgage Funding was the beneficiary of the trust deed, while AAG managed the loan account.In 2021, AAG claimed that the couple had relocated. The loan companies relied on this claim to declare a default on the reverse mortgage. They then hired Clear Recon Corp to begin foreclosure proceedings. Clear Recon used Aldridge Pite LLP to handle the legal notices.Aldridge Pite sent foreclosure notices addressed to Wallace from its office in Georgia. However, postal tracking records showed that the notices had neither reached the homeowners nor left Georgia. Clear Recon had access to these records but proceeded with the foreclosure sale in September 2022.Lantern Gate Properties bought the house at the auction. It subsequently filed an ejectment lawsuit against the couple, seeking to remove them from the property.Dispute over money left after the saleThe foreclosure sale generated more than $175,000 above the amount owed on the mortgage. This excess amount was meant to be available after the debt was accounted for. However, Clear Recon and Aldridge Pite withheld the money from the couple.Wallace and Barbara said they needed the funds to meet their regular living expenses. They also had to hire lawyers to obtain transaction records, check the sale figures and defend themselves against the eviction case.Their legal claims included allegations that Clear Recon and Aldridge Pite had misled them about the money. The couple said the companies told them the surplus could be released only if they signed a liability waiver.They also challenged the basis of the foreclosure, arguing that the loan companies had treated them as defaulters without confirming whether they had left the house. Their lawyers said the required notices had not been delivered and that the foreclosure sale was therefore invalid.What the companies arguedLantern Gate Properties maintained that it had bought the property in good faith at a public auction and held legal title to it. It argued that it was entitled to possession of the house.Clear Recon and Aldridge Pite denied the allegations of wrongdoing. They said they had followed standard foreclosure procedures. They also argued that legal documents and liability releases were required before the surplus funds could be distributed.AAG and Reverse Mortgage Funding did not present an active defence at the trial. The court had already found AAG liable by default on the couple's claims of financial abuse of a vulnerable person.What the jury decidedThe jury found Clear Recon liable on all three claims brought against it under Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act. It found that the company had willfully conducted the foreclosure sale when Wallace was not in default. It also found that Clear Recon had made false or misleading statements about the release of the surplus money and had refused to return it when the couple demanded it.The jury awarded Wallace $108,000 and Barbara $216,000 in actual damages against Clear Recon. It also ordered the company to pay $4.4 million in punitive damages. Separately, it awarded each of them $400,000 in economic damages and $250,000 in non-economic damages after finding the company liable for financial abuse of a vulnerable person.Aldridge Pite was also found liable under the Unlawful Trade Practices Act for misleading statements about the surplus funds and refusing to release the money on demand. The jury awarded each of the two homeowners $10,238 in actual damages and ordered the firm to pay $2.5 million in punitive damages.On the financial abuse claims against Aldridge Pite, the jury awarded each homeowner $250,000 in economic damages and another $250,000 in non-economic damages.AAG's liability had already been established by default. The jury awarded Wallace and Barbara $125,000 each in economic damages and $125,000 each in non-economic damages against the company.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Jordon Hudson sues Airbnb hosts, blaming them for shirtless Bill Belichick video
articles.summary: Airbnb hosts violated the privacy of Bill Belichick’s former girlfriend Jordon Hudson by leaking doorbell video of her shirtless, Super Bowl-winning boyfriend.
articles.body: Airbnb hosts violated the privacy of Bill Belichick’s former girlfriend by leaking unflattering doorbell video of her shirtless, Super Bowl-winning boyfriend three years ago, according to a lawsuit she filed Friday in Massachusetts civil court. Jordon Hudson claimed that hosts Elise McDevitt and Craig Nolan “exhibited no remorse or regard for these” actions taken outside the defendants’ Airbnb home in Winthrop. Hudson, now 25, and Belichick, 74, had wanted to keep their May-December romance under wraps when they checked into the defendants’ home for a four-night stay at 27 Brewster Ave. in summer 2023, the lawsuit said. During the final night of this getaway, McDevitt texted Hudson, asking her not to park in front of their neighbor’s home. That same message also included “a link to a Ring video of a shirtless Mr. Belichick walking to and from the Property, which had been captured and saved without the knowledge and authorization of Mr. Belichick or Ms. Hudson,” according to the lawsuit filed Friday. Hudson claimed that McDevitt agreed to delete the video only for it to hit social media later that year, making the plaintiff’s relationship with Belichick known to the public. McDevitt then reached out to Hudson, “out of the blue,” according to the lawsuit, in May 2025 and admitted to having shared the footage with friends, according to the civil complaint. “We had sent it to a few people initially wondering is this him [Mr. Belichick], isn’t it him and I don’t know what happened from there, but we did delete it from the camera, as I assured you,” McDevitt allegedly wrote to Hudson, according to the lawsuit. Hudson did not name a dollar amount she’s seeking. McDevitt and Nolan could not not immediately be reached by NBC News for comment on Monday via publicly listed phone numbers and email addresses. Representatives of Belichick, Ring and Airbnb also could not not be reached for comment on Monday, though none of them are named parties to the civil action. Boston civil attorney Michael Coyne said he doesn’t believe Hudson has any claim for damages because she and Belichick had no expectation of privacy while outside that Airbnb home. And furthermore, Coyne said, Hudson would be hard pressed to show how she was injured being outed as Belichick’s girlfriend. “So they misled you, they didn’t admit (leaking the video), as most defendants don’t. How have you been injured as a result of this?” said Coyne, chief legal analyst for NBC Boston and dean of the Massachusetts School of Law. “If anything, her profile was elevated by it. So where’s the damage?” Belichick and Hudson are no longer dating, according to multiple news outlets, and the North Carolina Tar Heels coach recently declined to refute those reports. Belichick is in his second year in Chapel Hill and his Tar Hells are 5-4 overall so far this season and 2-3 in ACC play. This season has been a bit of rebound from Belichick’s first year on campus in 2025 when UNC finished a disappointing 4-8 and 2-6. Belichick’s return to the college game following a phenomenal, 29-season NFL head coach career. His 467 victories ranks No. 3 in NFL history and his six Super Bowl rings with the New England Patriots are the most for any coach.

articles.title: Ohio State University investigating fraternity after video appears to show two people on fire
articles.summary: An Ohio State University fraternity is being investigated after video of two young men seemingly on fire circulated online over the weekend.
articles.body: An Ohio State University fraternity is being investigated after video of two young men seemingly on fire circulated online over the weekend. The Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity was placed on “interim suspension” pending a full investigation, according to a statement Sunday from OSU. The administration described it as an “extremely concerning incident” and noted that it referred the matter to law enforcement. “Ohio State is committed to a safe and healthy environment and expects students and student organizations to uphold that commitment and the university’s values,” the statement said. The video posted online starts with someone in a sweatsuit on the ground with his pants engulfed in flames. That individual gets up and tackles another person in a matching sweatsuit, resulting in the second person’s clothing being ignited. Both of the men then run around and attempt to shed their clothing while others come in to help them stamp out the flames, according to the video. A second video shot from a different angle appears to show that the second individual’s pant leg was already on fire when he was tackled. It also showed a bystander seemingly struggling to use a fire extinguisher as others tried to help snuff out the flames. The incident appeared to occur Saturday on a block near the university, according to a statement from the Columbus Police Department. There were no initial calls about the matter Saturday but the department was alerted Sunday about the video that was circulating online. “We will be working with the Ohio State University, as well as the Columbus Division of Fire’s Arson Unit to determine if any criminal acts occurred,” police said. Ohio State’s Buckeyes hosted the Oregon Ducks on Saturday as two of the NCAA’s top Division I football teams faced off. Many of the bystanders in the videos appeared to be wearing Ohio State football jerseys. The fraternity’s national headquarters is also aware of the video, Steve Mitchell, CEO of Sigma Alpha Epsilon, said in a statement to NBC News on Monday. Mitchell said that the fraternity is actively investigating the circumstances and working closely with the relevant authorities. “Sigma Alpha Epsilon holds its collegiate members to high standards of conduct and accountability,” Mitchell said. “Behavior that violates these standards has no place in our organization. We are committed to holding those responsible accountable and will take appropriate action based on the findings of the investigation.” Sigma Alpha Epsilon was founded March 9, 1856, at the University of Alabama. A number of notable figures have been members, such as former President William McKinley, author William Faulkner, actor Sam Elliot and NFL coach Pete Carroll. It has also had a concerning history of incidents over the last 20 years, culminating in a number of deaths, according to a 2013 Bloomberg report that dubbed it the “deadliest frat.” The report from Bloomberg noted that there were nine deaths related to drinking, drugs and hazing between 2006 and 2013, which it said was more than any other Greek organization. It added that more than 100 universities had disciplined Sigma Alpha Epsilon and 15 chapters had been shuttered. The national headquarters responded in 2014 by eliminating the pledge system, stating at the time that deaths and other incidents had resulted in “consequences that have never been consistent with our membership experience.” It replaced pledging with what it dubbed the “True Gentleman Experience,” referencing one of the organization’s guiding principles. The fraternity boasts that a true gentleman is defined in part by a man “whose conduct proceeds from good will and an acute sense of propriety.” There was an incident at a “talent show” held by the Sigma Alpha Epsilon chapter the University of New Hampshire in 2022 that resulted in 46 members being charged with hazing. While dozens chose to engage in diversion programs, three individuals were acquitted of the charges at trial, according to the New Hampshire Union Leader. The newspaper reported that the judge ruled that because the incident was not related to pledging or continued membership, it did not meet the requirement for a hazing charge under the law.

articles.title: Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.summary: The share price dropped wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from the value of Nvidia.
articles.body:
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 6% on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.

Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.

However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying "allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report .

The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.

The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.

Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.

"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."

After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.

US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".

However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.

While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened on a positive note on Monday after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.

But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so central to the AI industry.

"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.

Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.

Huang's position vulnerable unlike other tech bosses

A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.

Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.

He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.

By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.

Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."

The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.

Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.

What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

But Jensen Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

Additional reporter by Samira Hussain, North America business correspondent.

articles.title: Babydoll song had me leaping around the kitchen - Elton John
articles.summary: Sir Elton tells Cardiff native and Babydoll singer Jamie Miller that he has a "huge future" ahead.
articles.body:
Sir Elton John said he was "leaping around the kitchen" when he first heard Jamie Miller's history-making single, Babydoll.

Miller, from Pontprennau in Cardiff, became the first Welsh artist to top the UK singles chart in 15 years on 23 October with his viral TikTok hit, Babydoll - and the single has stayed there ever since, holding the top spot for over a fortnight.

Speaking on Sir Elton's Rocket Hour podcast, the Rocket Man singer told Miller he has a "huge future".

Sir Elton said: "As soon as I heard it [Babydoll] I was leaping around the kitchen. You really deserve the success because you sing like an angel. You have a huge future in front of you."

Babydoll was released on 7 August - months after Miller considered quitting music - but its success exploded after actress Jennifer Love Hewitt posted videos featuring the track.

Miller, who previously told BBC Wales his dad was an Uber driver in Cardiff, launched his career nearly a decade ago as a 19-year-old , after coming third on the sixth season of The Voice UK.

He is the first solo male Welsh artist in 41 years to top the singles chart, after Shakin' Stevens' 1985 festive hit, Merry Christmas Everyone.

Sir Elton said: "You must be thrilled with the way things are going at the moment.

"That record is so good and your voice is amazing.

"It's going to be huge all around the world.

"This is the start of the big career for you, and you should be so happy. It's a pop record - but it's a great record.

"There's no getting away with your talent, you're amazing."

Miller, who grew up in Cardiff and has lived in Los Angeles for about nine years, told Sir Elton: "When I was seven years old I used to sing all your songs, I wouldn't be the singer I am today if you didn't exist."

The 29-year-old has been nominated for a Nickelodeon Favourite Viral Song award at the Kids Choice Awards on 15 November.

"It's the first time I'm seeing my life change in real time," said Miller.

Miller said he was working on a "soulful, joyous and happy album that I feel like I've waited my whole life to write". He hopes it will be released at the beginning of 2027.

In addition, the singer is currently planning a world tour, with a promise to return to his roots and perform a number of shows in Wales.

articles.title: Meta rolls out automated age checks for teens globally
articles.summary: AI-powered scans will be used for Instagram accounts starting this month and later extended to Facebook and Threads.
articles.body:
Social media giant Meta is expanding automated age-estimation technology globally starting this month following billion-dollar legal settlements and criticism that its platforms fail to protect teenagers from online harms.

“We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections,” the company said in an announcement on Monday.

“Since first introducing this technology, we’ve been placing more teens in age-appropriate protections and are encouraged by the results. Based on that success, today we’re expanding this technology globally.”

Teen accounts have more restrictions and protections, limiting contacts, types of content and users’ time. Teens often circumvent the restrictions by creating a fake birthday when they set up an account, raising concerns that minors could bypass parental controls and be exposed to harmful content.

Parents in the United States who have set up Instagram for teenagers will receive notifications this month about the new measures. Meta said it will expand the age estimation algorithm to Facebook and Threads later in the year.

The AI technology, which the company has been testing in several countries, including the US, the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia, analyses user behaviour and posts to estimate the person’s age.

Parents can open accounts for children and categorise them as restricted teen accounts. But the age-estimation feature can also now automatically place accounts in the category, even if it was set up using a manually entered birthday that would have falsely made a user seem like an adult.

Meta has several categories of restrictions based on age. Children under 13 years of age are banned from using the apps. Teenagers are reminded to leave Instagram after 60 minutes of activity, and notifications are muted at night, when they would usually be sleeping.

Teen accounts face a two-hour-a-day usage limit as well, and are blocked from seeing “social comparison” features such as likes and reactions to other teen accounts.

The social media giant has faced growing legal action worldwide over how its platforms are used by teenagers. Child development experts have said platforms like Instagram and Facebook are highly addictive for young people, can reinforce social pressures through reactions to posts and expose them to other harmful content online.

Australia passed a ban on anyone below 16 years of age from using social media platforms last year. But this month, several groups, including the advocacy group Digital Freedom Project and the social media website Reddit, filed a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of that law, as well as the scientific rationale behind trying to keep children entirely off of platforms like YouTube, Facebook and TikTok.

In the US, Meta faced lawsuits from attorneys general across the US over the alleged harmful impact of its platforms on children, with Meta agreeing to improve how it identifies minors and children as part of the settlement.

The states alleged that Meta’s platforms “encourage addictive behaviour, fail to verify users’ ages, encourage adolescents to bypass parental controls, and inadequately safeguard against harmful content and/or intentionally amplify harmful and exploitative content”.

In August, the company agreed to pay $18bn to the states and institute a slew of changes to how it allows teenagers to interact with its platforms that could only be removed by parents or guardians.

The changes include restricting under-18 users to two hours a day on the platforms and enforcing a nighttime curfew from midnight to 6am. Default settings will restrict “social comparison” features such as seeing likes and reactions on posts, and “cosmetic procedure filters” that alter a person’s appearance. Push notifications will be blocked for teen accounts between 8am and 3pm, when they are likely to be in school.

Teen users will be encouraged to take breaks, with prompts appearing after every 15 minutes of continuous usage, and when daily usage hits 60 minutes and 90 minutes.

Parents and guardians will receive updates on teen account activities and be notified whenever they message an adult for the first time. Searches for topics like suicide, self-harm or eating disorders would also trigger a notification to parents.

In announcing the new automated age estimation on Monday, Meta also repeated calls for other industry leaders to implement similar changes.

“As Instagram is just one of the many apps teens use, we’re also calling on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to adopt these same practices to keep teens safe,” Meta said in its statement.

articles.title: France accuses Iran’s Revolutionary Guards of hacking supermarket refrigerators
articles.summary: French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot accused Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corp of being ⁠behind ​a ⁠recent cyberattack on ⁠French supermarket fridges.
articles.body: French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot on ⁠Monday accused Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corp of being ⁠behind ​a ⁠recent cyberattack on ⁠French supermarket fridges, ​saying there ⁠would ‌be consequences for the Islamic Republic. Meanwhile ‌the Paris ‌prosecutor’s office said it ⁠had requested international arrest warrants against the leader of Shahid Kaveh, an offensive ‌cyber unit ​affiliated ‌with the Revolutionary ⁠Guards, and ⁠his two ‌deputies. The hacks that struck hundreds of French supermarkets ⁠in early October were among the most disruptive cyberattacks of the Iran war that began in February, a conflict that has been marked by scattered incidents of alleged digital disruption. These have included hacks against the Los Angeles transit system in March, against U.S. water treatment plants in July and against ships bound for the United States in August. Iran’s mission to the United Nations did not return messages seeking comment. Iran routinely denies carrying out malicious cyber ⁠operations. Barrot said the Iranian ambassador had been summoned to France’s foreign ministry. He also threatened further European Union sanctions against Iran. The Oct. 11 cyberattack, which overrode the temperature controls on ⁠commercial fridges in hundreds of establishments, appeared to have been easy to pull off, cybersecurity experts previously told Reuters. The firm ​behind many ⁠of the stricken units said that several were obsolete ‌or were running outdated firmware, which could have made it easy for hackers to break in. The effects were still dramatic. Some refrigerators had the temperature turned up so high they caught fire. In the hours following the hack, supermarket employees carted boxes full ‌of perished meat and melted ice cream into giant trash containers. The attack’s total ‌costs could add up to tens of millions of euros nationwide, one French supermarket owner estimated. Reuters could not establish exactly how the French made their determination. The October hacks were followed this month by a second wave of hacking that hit more than 100 establishments across Europe and even affected refrigerators used by French blood banks, prompting ⁠employees there to have to move some of the blood to different cold storage units. The seemingly straightforward nature of the refrigerator hacks — and their repetition across multiple countries — prompted speculation about who might be responsible amid ongoing concerns over Russia’s suspected sabotage campaign in Europe, the war between the U.S. and Iran and the global rise of artificial intelligence powered cyberattacks. The sabotage of European supermarket fridges was preceded by at least one similar incident in the United States. In August, refrigerators in at least half a dozen military commissaries went out of commission. Pentagon investigators are treating the malfunctions as a suspected cyberattack and are working with French officials to get to the ‌bottom of what happened. It was unclear if there was any link between the attacks.

articles.title: Yemen government forces claim new advances as Houthi border attacks resume
articles.summary: Yemeni forces claim fresh advances across key fronts as cross-border Houthi attacks surge amid heavy clashes.
articles.body:
Yemen’s government forces have announced the capture of Houthi-held positions in the southern governorate of Lahj, amid fierce clashes with the Houthi rebels across multiple fronts in the country.

The government’s National Shield Forces said on Monday that they had seized positions on the al-Muhawala front in western Lahj after a large-scale assault on Houthi positions. The forces claimed that dozens of Houthi fighters had been killed or wounded in the attack.

The latest announcement comes after several days of reported gains by government forces in the northern governorate of al-Jawf, east of the Houthi-held Yemeni capital Sanaa. Government forces in al-Jawf have advanced in recent days through mountain ranges east of the provincial capital al-Hazm.

Al Jazeera Arabic reporter Suhaib al-Miyahi visited the al-Jawf front line on November 6, documenting trenches and fortifications in positions that government commanders said had been captured from the Houthis, as battles continued nearby.

The Houthis are continuing their attacks in Taiz, where they have encircled the city, imposing a siege on it for more than a month. Government forces say they have repelled Houthi attacks across several fronts in the outskirts of the city over the previous day.

In his daily update, government military spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili said on Monday that government forces had carried out almost 1,000 attacks in the previous hours, leaving more than 120 Houthi fighters dead or wounded. The claims could not be independently verified.

The recent clashes fall under the ongoing Operation Dawn of Yemen , which began on October 5 in an attempt to reverse Houthi gains made along the Red Sea coast the previous month, and eventually defeat the Iranian-backed rebel group.

However, Saudi-backed government forces have yet to make significant gains in what is proving to be a war of attrition, the latest phase of a more than decade-long war that began after the Houthi capture of Sanaa in September 2014.

Tawfik al-Hamidi, political analyst and president of the SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties, told Al Jazeera that the government is having some success in depleting Houthi manpower, partly as a result of the support it gets from Saudi air strikes.

“I believe that what is happening reflects a real depletion of the Houthis’ capabilities, and not just a tactical retreat,” al-Hamidi said.

He claimed that the number of Houthi attacks had decreased in frequency.

“The Houthi group still possesses military capabilities, but its ability to continue broad attacks and retain positions is facing mounting pressures,” al-Hamidi said.

He emphasised the strategic importance of al-Jawf because of its proximity to Sanaa, arguing that further government advances there could prompt the Houthis to redistribute their forces.

“I see that Taiz may be the biggest beneficiary of these developments, because it opens a real opportunity to ease the siege, leading to lifting it,” al-Hamidi said.

The escalation carries a severe humanitarian cost in Taiz, where nine civilians, including two children, were wounded in shelling and gunfire in several areas on Sunday, according to reports published on Monday by the state-run Saba news agency.

In a separate incident on Sunday, an ambulance came under fire in the al-Awat area, killing a wounded patient and his father and injuring a paramedic, according to local and medical sources cited by Saba.

The Joint Medical Emergency Committee in Taiz also said preliminary reports indicated that another ambulance had been targeted in the al-Shaqab area of Taiz.

The Houthis have meanwhile continued launching ballistic missiles and drones towards Saudi Arabia, including attacks targeting oil facilities.

The Saudi-led coalition said on Sunday that it had intercepted a drone and five missiles launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh and Saudi Arabia’s eastern and southern regions.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on Monday that Saudi forces had carried out more than 100 air strikes in the preceding 24 hours, targeting Marib, Sanaa, Hodeidah, Taiz, Lahj, and al-Jawf.

He alleged that the attacks had caused civilian casualties, but did not specify how many.

Al-Hamidi argued that the Houthis were using cross-border attacks to increase the security and economic costs of Saudi Arabia’s intervention, hoping to pressure Riyadh into halting the government offensive.

“The group realises that the continued advance of the government forces may weaken its military position, and therefore it uses missiles to raise the security and economic cost on Riyadh,” he explained.

But he warned that the strategy could backfire, prompting Saudi Arabia to instead intensify its military response rather than offering concessions.
